title: GnuTLS OCSP Stapling Revocation Verification Bypass
analysis:
### Source
Untrusted input arrives during the TLS handshake from a malicious or compromised TLS server presenting a revoked X.509 certificate and/or arbitrary/invalid OCSP stapling response.

### Sanitization/Validation
When an application configures `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` to require OCSP stapling validation (`config->verifystatus == TRUE`), libcurl built with GnuTLS (`lib/vtls/gtls.c`) attempts to check the certificate status.
At line 1147:
```c
if(gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked(session, 0) == 0) {
```
The logic assumes that if `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked(session, 0)` returns a non-zero value, GnuTLS has successfully verified the OCSP response.
However, in GnuTLS (particularly with TLS 1.3), `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked()` can return non-zero simply when the OCSP status extension was present in the handshake without GnuTLS actually verifying the signature, validity, or revocation status of the OCSP response.
Furthermore, if `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked(session, 0)` returns 0, curl enters the fallback block, parses the OCSP response, but unconditionally returns `CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS` at line 1241 even if the status is valid (`GNUTLS_OCSP_CERT_GOOD`). 
Thus, any time GnuTLS returns non-zero for `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked`, libcurl completely skips verifying the OCSP response and reports `"server certificate status verification OK"` (line 1244), accepting revoked certificates.

### Sink
At lines 1243-1245:
```c
    else
      infof(data, "  server certificate status verification OK");
```
The connection is established successfully without validating the OCSP response, allowing a man-in-the-middle attacker with a revoked certificate to bypass certificate revocation checks.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A man-in-the-middle server uses a revoked TLS certificate for the target hostname and completes a TLS 1.3 handshake with a client using libcurl with `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` enabled and GnuTLS backend. The server includes an unverified/dummy OCSP status response extension. `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked()` returns non-zero, causing curl to bypass OCSP verification and complete the TLS connection.

title: ASN.1 GeneralizedTime Parsing Integer Underflow and Out-of-Bounds Read in GTime2str
analysis:
### Source
Untrusted input enters via an X.509 server certificate received during a TLS handshake from an untrusted remote server.

### Sanitization/Validation
In `Curl_extract_certinfo` (`lib/vtls/x509asn1.c`), certificate dates (`notBefore` and `notAfter`) are parsed using `ASN1tostr`, which delegates ASN.1 GeneralizedTime elements (`CURL_ASN1_GENERALIZED_TIME`) to `GTime2str`. The function checks that there are at least 12 digits for the timestamp prior to any decimal separator (`switch(fracp - beg - 12)`). However, when a fractional delimiter (`.` or `,`) is present, it does not check whether there are actually any fractional digits following the delimiter.

### Sink
In `GTime2str`, if a GeneralizedTime value ends with `.` or is immediately followed by a timezone specifier like `Z` (e.g., `20240101000000.Z` or `20240101000000.`), `tzp` and `fracp` will point to the exact same character (`Z` or `end`).
At line 523:
```c
for(fracl = tzp - fracp - 1; fracl && fracp[fracl - 1] == '0'; fracl--)
```
Since `tzp - fracp == 0`, evaluating `0 - 1` on the unsigned `size_t` variable `fracl` underflows to `SIZE_MAX` (`(size_t)-1`). 
First, evaluating `fracp[fracl - 1]` triggers an out-of-bounds heap read (`fracp + SIZE_MAX - 1`).
Second, if `fracp[SIZE_MAX - 1]` is not `'0'`, `fracl` retains `SIZE_MAX`. 
At line 540-545:
```c
return Curl_dyn_addf(store, "%.4s-%.2s-%.2s %.2s:%.2s:%c%c%s%.*s%s%.*s",
                     beg, beg + 4, beg + 6,
                     beg + 8, beg + 10, sec1, sec2,
                     fracl? ".": "", (int)fracl, fracp,
                     sep, (int)tzl, tzp);
```
`(int)fracl` casts `SIZE_MAX` to `(int)-1`. When passed to `vsnprintf` via `Curl_dyn_addf`, a negative precision specifier for `%.*s` is treated according to C standards as an omitted precision specifier (equivalent to `%s`). Because `fracp` points inside a raw ASN.1 DER buffer without a null terminator, `vsnprintf` reads past the buffer bounds in heap memory until an arbitrary NUL byte is found, causing out-of-bounds memory reading, heap data leakage into `store`, or a denial-of-service crash (SIGSEGV).

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A malicious TLS server responds to a curl request with an X.509 certificate whose `notBefore` or `notAfter` validity field contains an ASN.1 GeneralizedTime string (tag `0x18`) with value:
`20240101000000.Z` (hex bytes: `18 10 32 30 32 34 30 31 30 31 30 30 30 30 30 30 2e 5a`)
When libcurl connects to the server (e.g. using GnuTLS, Schannel, SecureTransport, or with `CURLOPT_CERTINFO` enabled), `Curl_extract_certinfo` invokes `ASN1tostr` on the validity dates of the leaf certificate (`certnum == 0`), underflowing `fracl` and triggering the out-of-bounds heap read.

title: Stack Out-of-Bounds Read in mac_idn_to_ascii and mac_ascii_to_idn via Non-Null-Terminated ICU Buffer
analysis:
### Source
Untrusted user input enters via a URL hostname (e.g. from an HTTP redirect `Location:` header or direct user-provided URL with an internationalized domain name).

### Sanitization/Validation
In `mac_idn_to_ascii` (and `mac_ascii_to_idn`) in `lib/idn.c`, the hostname is passed to Apple's `icucore` library function `uidna_nameToASCII_UTF8` (or `uidna_nameToUnicodeUTF8`) with a stack buffer `char buffer[256]`.
The code checks error return using `U_FAILURE(err)`.
However, according to ICU specification, if the resulting converted domain name exactly fills the 256-byte destination buffer (`destCapacity == resultLength`), ICU does not null-terminate `buffer`, and sets the error code to `U_STRING_NOT_TERMINATED_WARNING` (value `-124`).
Because `U_FAILURE(code)` is defined in ICU as `((code) > 0)`, warnings (which have negative integer values) are not treated as failures. Therefore, `U_FAILURE(err)` evaluates to `FALSE` (0).

### Sink
At lines 74-75:
```c
*out = strdup(buffer);
```
`buffer` is completely filled with 256 non-null bytes and lacks a null terminator. `strdup(buffer)` performs an out-of-bounds stack read past the end of `buffer[256]`, reading adjacent stack memory until an arbitrary null byte is encountered. This leads to information disclosure of stack memory into the heap allocation `*out`, or an application crash (SIGSEGV) if unmapped stack boundary memory is read.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A malicious HTTP server redirects curl using a `Location` header to an internationalized domain name whose UTF-8 punycode conversion results in exactly 256 bytes (e.g., `Location: http://<label-encoded-to-256-punycode-chars>/`).
When libcurl processes the redirect on macOS/iOS with `USE_APPLE_IDN` enabled, `Curl_idn_decode` calls `mac_idn_to_ascii`, which invokes `uidna_nameToASCII_UTF8` and then `strdup` on the unterminated stack buffer.
